items.text: Restrict $E\mapsto\tilde E$ to a smaller class of fibre spaces so as to get a fully faithful functor.
Over a point: discrete spaces. A discrete space = its underlying set.
\{\text{discrete spaces}\}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \operatorname{Top}(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbf{Sets}\qquad\text{(tautological)}
Étale spaces
Generalise to a base $X$: « discrete relative to $X$ » = étale over $X$.
$\pi\colon E\to X$ continuous is étale (a local isomorphism) if
\forall\, x\in E\ \ \exists\ \text{open } V\ni x:\quad \pi(V)\ \text{open in } X,\quad \pi|_V\colon V\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\pi(V)\ \text{homeomorphism}
$E$ is covered by open sets on each of which $\pi$ is an open immersion.
Old terminology: « domaines étalés » (functions of one complex variable). Purely topological notion.
No English word; « local homeomorphism » hides that $\pi(V)$ is open, and does not carry over to differentiable / analytic / algebraic settings.
Examples
1. $U\hookrightarrow X$ an open subset: the model of an étale map.
2. $I$ a discrete set: $I\times X\to X$, the projection.
I\times X=\coprod_{i\in I}X\ \longrightarrow\ X
Covered by $|I|$ open copies of $X$, each mapped homeomorphically: étale.
3. Covering spaces: locally over $X$, isomorphic to $U\times I$ with $I$ discrete.
Theorem
$\operatorname{Et}(X)$ = full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fib}(X)$ of étale spaces.
\operatorname{Et}(X)\ \xrightarrow{\ E\mapsto\tilde E\ }\ \operatorname{Top}(X)\quad\text{is an equivalence of categories}
Proof not given here (half an hour to an hour): the aim is the main ideas. In Godement.
A dictionary: sheaf as sections over open sets $\leftrightarrow$ étale space over $X$.
The quasi-inverse is awkward to write down.
Some operations are convenient in one language, some in the other: learn to juggle between them.
An example: $z\mapsto z^n$
Riemann surfaces: étale except at the ramification points.
f\colon \mathbf C\to\mathbf C,\qquad x\mapsto x^n\quad(n\ge 2)
Fibre over $x_0\ne 0$: the $n$ roots of $x_0$, i.e. $n$ points $y_1,\dots,y_n$ (multiply by the $n$-th roots of unity).
f\colon \mathbf C^{*}\to\mathbf C^{*}\quad\text{is étale}
Over $\mathbf C^{*}$ it is a covering space; at $0$ it is not étale.
Inverse limits in a category
A diagram $D$ in $C$ of type $d$: objects $D_i$, arrows $D(\varphi)$ for $\varphi$ in the type. Inverse limit in $\mathbf{Sets}$ = coherent systems $(x_i)_i$ with $x_i\in D_i$.
\prod_{i}D_i\ \rightrightarrows\ \prod_{\varphi}D_{\text{target}(\varphi)}
(x_i)\ \longmapsto\ \bigl(x_{\text{target}(\varphi)}\bigr)_\varphi\quad\text{and}\quad \bigl(D(\varphi)\,x_{\text{source}(\varphi)}\bigr)_\varphi
\varprojlim D=\ker\Bigl(\prod_i D_i\rightrightarrows\prod_\varphi D_{\text{target}(\varphi)}\Bigr)
Hence: products + kernels of pairs of arrows $\Rightarrow$ all inverse limits.
Finite products (the empty one included) + kernels $\Rightarrow$ limits over finite diagrams.
Valid in any category $C$: the limit exists iff this pair of arrows has a kernel. Or reduce to products and fibre products.
The enlargement $\hat C$
In $\operatorname{Hom}(C^{\circ},\mathbf{Sets})$ inverse limits exist and are computed componentwise.
i\colon C\to\hat C,\qquad X\mapsto h_X=\operatorname{Hom}(-,X)\quad\text{fully faithful}
A diagram in $C$ is a diagram in $\hat C$; its limit there always exists.
It exists in $C$ iff the limit in $\hat C$ is in the essential image of $C$ (representable).
$\hat C$: the natural enlargement of $C$; it will turn out to be a topos.
Sheaves among presheaves
$C=\mathcal O(X)$: then $\hat C$ = presheaves on $X$.
\operatorname{Top}(X)\subset \hat{\mathcal O}\quad\text{full subcategory}
Three possibilities for limits in a full subcategory $F\subset E$: they may not exist in $F$; exist but differ; or exist and coincide.
Third case: $F$ is stable under limits taken in $E$.
This is what happens for sheaves in presheaves.
Sheaves are defined by left exactness conditions (isomorphisms between kernels of pairs of arrows); limits commute with limits.
So inverse limits of sheaves exist and are computed as for presheaves, componentwise.
(F\times G)(U)=F(U)\times G(U)
\ker(u,v)(U)=\ker\bigl(F(U)\rightrightarrows G(U)\bigr),\qquad u,v\colon F\rightrightarrows G
Again a sheaf: it is the kernel in sheaves.
Limits of étale spaces
$E$, $F$ étale over $X$. Product in $\operatorname{Fib}(X)$:
E\times_X F=\{(e,f): \pi(e)=\pi'(f)\}\subset E\times F
Étale: cover by $U_i\times_X V_j\simeq U_i\cap V_j$, open in $X$.
Same for a finite number of factors; false for infinite products: this geometric description works only for finite limits.
Kernel of $u,v\colon E\rightrightarrows F$ over $X$:
\ker(u,v)=\{e\in E: u(e)=v(e)\}\ \ \text{open in } E
Two maps over $X$ equal at a point agree near it, so the kernel is open, hence étale.
Algebraic structures
With finite products, a law on an object $X$ is a morphism $X\times X\to X$.
m\colon X\times X\to X
Associative, unit, group, ring, module, algebra... all expressible by commutative diagrams.
Hence in sheaves: a sheaf of groups, of rings, of modules over a sheaf of rings.
Direct limits
Dual notion: $\varinjlim_D$ in $C$ = $\varprojlim_{D^{\circ}}$ in $C^{\circ}$.
$L$ with arrows $D_i\to L$ making the triangles commute, universal.
D(\varphi)\colon D_i\to D_j,\qquad D_i\to L,\ D_j\to L
\operatorname{Hom}(L,Z)\longrightarrow \varprojlim_i \operatorname{Hom}(D_i,Z)
